Ugarit's plea for help saved nothing. One of its songs got through.

So that's how one city died. Now the first question, which everyone asks. Who did it?

The old answer was the Sea Peoples: one great wave of invaders rolling down the coast, burning every city in a single terrible year. I told you last time why I don't believe in the wave. Here's what the ground says.

It took about fifty years. A child born when the first palace burned could have died of old age before the last one did.

And it was a patchwork. A few years ago an archaeologist named Jesse Millek did something nobody had done. He took every city that the textbooks say was destroyed in this period, a hundred and fifty-three claims, and he went back to the original dig reports for each one. About six in ten fell apart. Some had been dated wrong by a century. Some had burned in one building and not the rest. Some had no evidence at all, only a line in one book that had been copied into the next.

So some cities burned. Some were emptied without a fight. Some carried on. And the ones that did burn weren't all burned by the same people.

Let me take you to three of them.

The first is a town called Emar, on the Euphrates in Syria. It's about as far from the sea as you can get in that country. No ship ever reached it. And it fell around 1185.

Before it fell its scribes left us the sound of a city going under, and it isn't screaming. It's paperwork. They kept drawing up contracts in the proper form, with witnesses and seals, and a group of those contracts all start with the same phrase: "in the year of distress."

In the year of distress, a man sold his house. In the year of distress, a man sold himself. One tablet records what grain cost while the town was under siege, and it's about a day's food for a shekel of silver, which was a month's wages.

And there's one contract I find very hard to read. A couple sold their children. Four of them: two girls and two boys, the youngest still nursing. The contract says why. It was the year of distress and they couldn't feed them. The buyer was a man with a full storehouse.

A child can't sign a contract or roll a seal. So the scribe took lumps of damp clay and pressed each child's foot into one, and wrote the child's name beside the print.

Those survive. You can see the toes.

The scribes of Emar had a set phrase for catastrophe because it had become ordinary enough to need one.

The second is the Hittite capital, and it's the one that surprised the archaeologists most.

For a century people assumed it was stormed and sacked. More careful digging told a different story. The palace and the temples had been cleared out before they burned. There were no bodies and no treasure. The royal seals were gone and so were the statues of the gods.

The court had packed up and left. They took what a government needs to keep being a government: the seals that make a document official, the gold, and the gods, because you don't leave the gods. They left behind what they couldn't carry and didn't need, which was the past. Thousands of old tablets, treaties and letters and records going back four hundred years, still on the shelves.

Where they went, nobody knows. Some later time the empty city burned.

So the empire that had fought Egypt to a standstill didn't go down in a last battle. Its government walked out of its own capital one season and was never heard from again. And because they took their current files and left their archives, we can read four centuries of Hittite history and we can't find the ending.

One branch of that family did survive. Down on the Euphrates, in a city the Hittites had ruled through a line of royal cousins, the cousins carried on. Within a generation their king was calling himself Great King. The title was vacant, so he took it.

The third is Pylos, in Greece, and you know someone there.

Around 1180 BCE the palace burned, and nobody rebuilt it. We don't know who set the fire. It might have been raiders from the sea. It might have been the kingdom next door, or the palace's own hungry subjects. It didn't have walls.

Here's the part I told you to remember. The Counter's tablets were damp clay, meant to be wiped at the end of the year. They were on the shelf in the archive room when the roof came down in flames. The fire baked them. Clay that would have been mud by spring turned to brick, and it lay in the ruins for thirty-one centuries until an American team dug it out in 1939.

Everything I've told you about Pylos comes from that one fire: the figs, the weaving women, the bronze issued to the smiths. We have the last year's accounts of that kingdom only because the kingdom was destroyed.

And you remember what was in those accounts. Eight hundred men assigned to watch the coast.

Somewhere on that shore was a man on a headland, with a handful of others, looking at the water. We don't know if he saw anything. The tablet says where he was posted. It doesn't say what came.

The other Greek palaces went in the same decades. And there's a detail that complicates the picture of total ruin. At Tiryns, the one with the giant walls, the palace burned. But the town below it grew afterward. People moved in from the countryside and put up new houses in rows under the old citadel. They never rebuilt the palace, and they kept no accounts. They went on living there, without a king, for another hundred years.

Now Egypt, because Egypt is where the wave finally broke.

In 1177 BCE the king of Egypt was Ramses the Third, and he's the one who left the famous description. It's carved on the wall of his temple, and it's the nearest thing we have to an ancient account of the whole collapse.

"The foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands. All at once the lands were removed and scattered in the fray. No land could stand before their arms."

Then he lists the ones that had fallen: the Hittites, the south coast of Turkey, Cyprus, and others. He says the enemy set up camp in Syria and came on toward Egypt "while the flame was prepared before them."

He met them twice. There was a battle on land, somewhere on the coast road, and a battle on the water, in the mouths of the Nile. He'd lined the banks with archers and let the enemy ships come in close. Both are shown on the temple wall in huge detail. He won both.

Two things about those carvings.

The first is that his list isn't accurate. He names the Hittite cousins' city on the Euphrates among the fallen, and it hadn't fallen. A king's inscription is advertising. When it disagrees with the ground, I go with the ground.

The second is in the picture of the land battle. In among the fighting men there are ox-carts, heavy ones with solid wheels. There are women in the carts, and small children being lifted down out of the way of the fighting.

That's a migration. Those are families who'd put everything they had on a cart and walked south, because wherever they'd come from, they couldn't live there any more. I can't know what they'd seen. I think of the Farmer, though, and the seed jar. I think some of the people on those carts had been farmers in Turkey or on the islands, three bad years earlier.

Egypt didn't drive them all into the sea. It settled a lot of them in its own fortress towns on the coast of Canaan, as garrison troops, on rations. One group in particular, the Peleset. In a few generations they'll have five cities of their own down there, and their neighbors in the hills will call them Philistines.

So Egypt won. Here's what winning looked like twenty years later.

On the west bank of the Nile there was a village where the craftsmen lived who cut and painted the royal tombs. They were skilled men, paid by the state in grain. In about 1157 BCE their grain was eighteen days late. So they put down their tools, walked out past the guard posts and sat down behind one of the temples, and they wouldn't move.

A scribe wrote down what they said. We've come here because we're hungry and thirsty. There's no clothing, no oil, no fish, no vegetables. Write to Pharaoh about it.

It's the first strike in recorded history. They got some of their back pay, and then it happened again, and again. The richest state in the world could no longer reliably pay the men who dug its kings' graves. Within a generation those same villagers were on trial for robbing the tombs their grandfathers had built, and we have their confessions.

And the king who beat the Sea Peoples? There was a plot in his own household. One of his wives wanted her son on the throne. We have the court record of the trial, with the sentences. It doesn't say whether the plot succeeded. In 2012 his mummy was put through a CT scanner. His throat had been cut to the bone.

Egypt survived. It kept its river, its temples and its writing, which is more than most. But the empire in Syria was gone, and the gold that used to go north bought nothing now, because there was nobody to send it to.

One more, far to the east, where no sea raider ever went. Around 1158 BCE the king of Elam, in southwestern Iran, came down on Babylon and ended the mountain dynasty that had ruled it for four hundred years. Babylon had no sea coast. Whatever was squeezing these kingdoms wasn't only coming from the sea.

That king of Elam liked souvenirs. He carried home the great monuments of Iraq's past. He took the victory stone of Naram-Sin, the king with the horns. And he took a seven-foot pillar of black stone covered in laws.

That's why Hammurabi's pillar was found in Iran. The first two empires of this story ended up as loot from the wreck of the third, side by side in the same storeroom. They're still side by side, in the same room in Paris.

So who did it? That's the wrong kind of question, the kind that looks for one culprit. The drought was real. The raiders were real. There were earthquakes, and revolts, and kings who made bad decisions. Any one of those, a healthy world could have taken. The horse kingdom's fall proved it.

What killed this world is that the parts had come to depend on each other so completely that they couldn't fail one at a time. A palace needed its smiths, the smiths needed ships, the ships needed safe harbors, the harbors needed armies, and the armies needed grain. Pull one out in a bad decade and the rest went down in order. The thing that made them rich is the thing that made the fall total.

A world of villages like the first house can't fall like that. This one could.

Now the family, one at a time, because each of them lost something different.

The Keeper is gone. There's no Great King of the Hittites. There's no king at Ugarit, or Pylos, or Mycenae. Egypt has one, with his throat cut. The men who called each other brother have no one left to write to.

The Counter has a skill nobody is hiring. In Greece his whole profession existed because one palace needed accounts. The palace is ash. There's nothing to count, no one to pay him, and no pupil to teach. He can still read. There's nothing to read.

The Carrier has ships, and no ports that are safe and no partners who answer. Some of his line, I suspect, are the people on the other side of this story now. A merchant captain with a crew, no cargo and a hungry family is not far from being a raider.

The Maker has no tin. So he does what you'd do. He melts down what's broken. A cracked pot, a bent blade, the hinges off a burned door. All over this world archaeologists find little stashes of scrap bronze from these years, weighed out and buried under a floor like savings. Every one of them belonged to somebody who thought things would get back to normal.

Chariots went with him, by the way. A chariot needs a stable, a workshop, a trainer and a king. Men on foot with javelins and long swords could deal with what was left of them.

The Farmer is alive. That's the first thing. There are fewer of him, and I can't tell you how many fewer, and I won't guess. But he never depended on tin or treaties to do his job. The collector who used to take a third of his barley hasn't come this year. In some places the Farmer put his family on a cart, and in some he walked up into the hills where nobody had ever bothered to farm. We'll follow him there.

And his sister.

This is the third question, and it's the one I can't answer.

She's been in the story since the first house, at the grinding stone. Then in the weaving sheds of Uruk, as a number. Then in the lists at Ur, fifteen thousand of her. Then in the merchant's contracts, and on the ration tablets at Pylos, labelled "captives."

What happened to those women when the palace burned?

We don't know, and the reason matters. The only reason we ever knew they existed is that the institution that owned them kept a list. The list was the only witness to their lives. When the institution died, the list stopped.

Maybe some of them walked away free. That's possible. The thing that held them was gone. Maybe some died in the fire. Maybe some were taken by whoever burned the place and sold again somewhere else, into a ledger nobody kept. No document anywhere says.

For four thousand years they were counted and never named. At the end they weren't even counted.

I don't have anything to offer about that except to say it out loud.

By 1150 BCE it's quiet.

The ships aren't coming. Nobody is writing letters in Babylonian to kings three months away, because there's nobody at the other end. From Greece to the Euphrates, people are living on what they can grow within a day's walk, defend with their own hands, and make from what's lying around.

And they're telling stories. In Greece the palaces are empty, and there's nobody left who can read the old accounts. But people remember that there were kings once, in great halls, with bronze armor and chariots, who sailed across the sea to a war. Nobody remembers the tax records. They remember the heroes.

That's all that's left of the Greek palaces for the next four hundred years: a story, getting better every time it's told.

The Hittites didn't even get that.

Next time, the world afterward. I'd always heard it called a dark age. I'm not sure that's the right word, and I'll tell you why.


# Part 8 — After

Somewhere around the year 1000 BCE a man is grazing goats under a wall.

He's in the south of Greece, below the hill of Tiryns. The wall above him is twenty-five feet thick and made of stones the size of oxcarts, fitted together without mortar. It's been standing empty since before his great-grandfather was born.

He knows who built it. Everybody knows. Giants built it. One-eyed giants, called Cyclopes, because no men could have lifted those stones.

He's wrong, and you know he's wrong, because you watched tired farmers build that wall two parts ago. They were his own ancestors, seven or eight generations back. But look at it from where he stands. Nobody he's ever met could build that. Nobody he's ever met has heard of anyone who could. A wall that size needs an explanation, and giants fit the facts he has.

It's Xenophon again, six hundred years early. When the knowledge goes, a story moves in. And archaeologists still call that kind of stonework Cyclopean.

So that's where we are. A hundred and eighty years after the fires, in a Greece that has forgotten its own palaces. I want to ask four questions about this world, and the first is the one that herder raises.

How do you forget how to read?

It seems impossible. Once people can write, how does a whole country stop? But follow the Counter's line at Pylos and you'll see that nothing could be easier. I'm making up the family. The arithmetic is real.

The grandfather is the clerk at the desk by the palace door. He knows about ninety signs. He learned them the only way anyone could, by sitting at an older clerk's elbow in that room. There were no schools. There was nothing to read for pleasure. In all the Greek writing that survives from that age there isn't one line of poetry, and not one letter. The script was for accounts.

The palace burns when his son is about fifteen and half trained. The son gets away. He lives another forty years in a country where there's nothing to record and nobody who'd pay him to record it. He remembers some of the signs. He never uses them.

The grandson is a farmer. He's heard there used to be a palace. He's never seen a tablet, and nobody ever showed him a sign.

That's all it takes: three generations and nobody to practice on. A skill that has one employer dies with the employer. Greece would go four hundred years without writing anything down, and when Greeks wrote again it was in a completely different script that came from somewhere else.

Second question. Why didn't they just rebuild?

The stones were still there. The fields were still there. Plenty of people were alive who remembered how things used to run. Why not put it back?

Because a palace wasn't a building. It was an arrangement between specialists, and each one needed all the others to already be in place. Think of a town with one big factory. The factory closes. The machinists don't open a new factory. They can't. They'd need the suppliers and the customers and the bank and the rail line, and those all left when the factory did.

The Maker can't cast bronze without tin. The tin can't come without the Carrier's ship. The ship won't sail without a safe port at the other end. The port needs a king to guard it, the king needs chariots, and the chariots need the Maker. Take away any one piece and the others would have to wait for it. They were all taken away at once.

So people did the sensible thing. They got smaller.

Archaeologists count the places in Greece where people were living in 1250 BCE, and the places where they were living two centuries later, and the second number is about a quarter of the first. Now, that's a count of sites, and small poor villages are easy to miss. I don't believe three Greeks in four died. But a lot did, and a lot left, and the ones who stayed lived in hamlets of a few dozen, in houses of mud and thatch, and buried their dead with a pot and a pin.

And yet it wasn't empty, and I want to show you the place that proves it.

On the island of Euboea, at a village called Lefkandi, a bulldozer cut into a low mound in 1980. Under it was a building a hundred and fifty feet long. Nothing that size was supposed to exist in Greece for another two hundred years. It had been put up around 950 BCE over two graves.

In one was a man's ashes, wrapped in cloth and placed in a bronze jar. The jar was an antique from Cyprus, already a century old. Next to him lay a woman with gold on her dress and at her throat a gold necklace that had been made in Babylon about a thousand years before she was born. In the pit beside them were four horses.

So in the darkest part of the dark age, somebody on that island was rich. They had things from Cyprus and from Iraq. They could get a hundred people to put up the biggest building in the country. And they buried their chief the way heroes get buried in a poem that nobody had written down yet.

The Keeper's line isn't dead, then. It's just shrunk back to where it started. And here's a detail I like a great deal. In the palace accounts at Pylos there's a title for a very minor official, a kind of local foreman. It turns up, among other places, in charge of small groups of bronze smiths. The word is basileus. The great lords who ran the palaces had a different, grander title, and after the fires that title vanishes. The foreman's title doesn't. By the time Greeks are writing again, basileus is their word for king.

The kings of the Greek dark age were the descendants of the palace's foremen. They were the highest-ranking people left.

Now I want you to meet a real person from these years, because there's one document that shows the new world better than any amount of digging.

Around 1075 BCE an official of the great temple in southern Egypt was sent on a business trip. His name was Wenamun. His job was to sail to the port of Byblos, on the coast of Lebanon, and buy cedar logs for the sacred boat of the god Amun. We have his report. Scholars argue about whether it's a real report or a story written in the form of one. Either way, somebody who knew that world wrote it.

You've heard of Byblos. Three hundred years earlier its king was the man who wrote to Egypt sixty times, begging for a few archers, calling himself a bird in a trap, throwing himself at Pharaoh's feet seven times and seven times more. Keep that in your head.

Wenamun's trip goes wrong at once. He stops at a harbor on the way, a town now run by one of the peoples who'd come with the sea raiders. One of his own crew steals the money he's carrying and runs. Wenamun goes to the local chief and demands his money back. The chief points out, quite reasonably, that the thief was Wenamun's own man. Nobody helps him.

He gets to Byblos with almost nothing. The prince of Byblos sends a message down to the harbor: get out of my port. He sends the same message the next day. He sends it every day for twenty-nine days.

Finally Wenamun is let in. He describes the scene. The prince is sitting in an upstairs room with his back to a window, and through the window Wenamun can see the waves of the sea breaking behind the prince's head.

And the prince asks him some questions. Where are your letters of introduction? Where's the ship Egypt gave you for the timber? What have you brought to pay for it?

Then he has his clerks bring out the old account books, rolls and rolls of them, and read aloud what earlier pharaohs sent in exchange for cedar. Six shiploads of goods, last time. He says: if the king of Egypt were my master, he would have sent silver and gold. I am not your servant. And I am not the servant of the man who sent you.

That's the prince of Byblos talking to Egypt. Three hundred years after the bird in the trap.

In the end Wenamun has to write home for money. Egypt sends gold, silver, linen, ox hides, rope, sacks of lentils, baskets of fish, and five hundred rolls of papyrus. The timber gets cut. And then, just as he's about to leave, eleven ships turn up from the town where he was robbed, with orders to arrest him. He sits down on the beach and cries. The prince, who by this point seems to feel sorry for him, sends down two jars of wine, a sheep, and an Egyptian singing-girl to cheer him up.

The papyrus breaks off before we find out whether he got home.

It's the best single document we have from the age after the collapse. The great power has to pay cash in advance, and the little port keeps the books.

One footnote. Those five hundred rolls of papyrus were Byblos's main import, for centuries. So much of it came through that town that the Greeks named the stuff after it. Their word for a papyrus roll, and then for a book, was byblos. That's where the word Bible comes from.

That prince and his neighbors along the coast are the Carrier's line, and they came through.

They came through because they were small and they floated. Their towns had never carried the weight of a big palace and a chariot army, and they'd always lived off the sea. When the kings disappeared, there was nobody left to tell them where they could sail. Within two centuries the ships of Tyre and Sidon and Byblos were working the whole Mediterranean, as far as Spain. They planted a trading post in North Africa that grew into Carthage. They sold cedar, and a purple dye made from sea snails that was worth more than silver. The Greeks called them Phoenicians, which seems to mean the purple people.

So the Carrier doesn't work for a king any more. He works for himself.

Third question, and it's the one people argue about. Was the dark age dark?

Go to the Farmer, because he's moved. He's in the hills of Canaan now, the spine of high ground that runs down the middle of what's today Israel and the West Bank.

Before the collapse almost nobody lived up there. The towns were all on the plain, under local kings who answered to Egypt, and the hills were rough scrub with no springs. An Israeli archaeologist named Israel Finkelstein organized a survey in the 1980s, teams walking the ridges and picking up broken pottery, and the numbers came out like this. Before 1200 BCE, about thirty settlements in those hills. Two centuries later, about two hundred and fifty.

They're small. A dozen houses, mostly. The houses are stone, with a few rooms around a yard, and the ground floor is for the animals. There are pits cut in the rock for storing grain and cisterns lined with plaster to catch the winter rain. The hillsides are cut into terraces, which is backbreaking work.

And look at what isn't there. There are no palaces. There are no temples to speak of. There are no rich graves and hardly any imported goods. Everybody's pots are about the same.

Who were they? That's argued. Finkelstein himself thinks many were herders who settled down when the towns they used to trade with fell apart. Others think they were farmers from the plain who moved uphill to get out from under what was left of the kings. Their pottery is ordinary Canaanite pottery, so they weren't newcomers from far away. And that monument I mentioned from 1208 already has a people called Israel living somewhere in this country. Some of these villagers will become the Israelites of the Bible.

Now, here's the case for calling this a release. The Farmer keeps what he grows. For three thousand years, somebody has come at harvest and taken a share: the temple, the governor, the palace. Up here nobody comes. Terraces scattered over a ridge are a tax collector's nightmare. You can't see them from a road, you can't tell what they yielded, and it isn't worth the climb. His sons aren't called up to haul stone, and his sister isn't on a list.

And here's the case against, because I don't want to sell you a fairy tale. There's also no granary on the hill above him that opens in a famine. There's no garrison between him and the next valley, and the next valley is hungry too. The Bible's own book about these centuries is called Judges, and it's one of the most violent books in the collection: raids, massacres, a civil war. It has a line it keeps repeating. In those days there was no king in Israel, and every man did what was right in his own eyes. It isn't meant as praise.

So was it dark? From a palace, yes, because there's nothing there a palace would recognize. From the Farmer's doorway I think it was lighter and more dangerous at once. He was freer than his grandfather, and he had less of a net under him. People in that position usually want a king back within a few generations, and these did.

Down on the coast below him, the other half of that story is settling in.

At a handful of towns on the southern plain, the pottery changes after the collapse. It's painted in the style of the Greek palaces, with birds and spirals. But it's made of local clay. That matters. Imported pots mean trade. Foreign-style pots made on the spot mean foreign potters who've moved in.

These are the Peleset, the ones Egypt fought and then settled. They brought their own cooking pots and their own kind of hearth. They ate pork, and you can see it in their trash, while up in the hill villages there are almost no pig bones at all. A few years ago researchers got DNA from the bones of people buried in one of those coastal towns. The earliest burials after the collapse have a clear dose of ancestry from southern Europe. Two centuries later it's faded to nothing. They'd married into the neighborhood.

In the Bible these are the Philistines, and they're the villains: the people of Goliath, the enemies of David. I find it oddly moving that both sides of that old quarrel came out of the same disaster. The hill farmers and the coast people were both washed up by the fall of the palaces. Neither of them knew it.

Now the Maker, because he's found something to do.

You know his problem. There's no tin. He's been melting scrap, and every time he recasts it there's a little less.

On Cyprus, the copper island, the smiths had known about iron for a long time as a curiosity. In the 1100s they start making real tools out of it. The earliest ones are a nice thing to look at: knives with an iron blade, held to the handle by bronze rivets. It's the old metal and the new one in the same object.

Why then? The usual answer is that the tin stopped coming and they had no choice. I think that's partly right. But Cyprus went on making bronze through the whole crisis, so it can't be only that. I think it's also that the Maker was on his own. He had no palace telling him what to make and none supplying him, and iron has one enormous advantage that had never mattered before. The ore is everywhere. You don't need a ship or a treaty or a king, only a hillside, a lot of charcoal, and patience.

It wasn't better at first. Raw iron is softer than good bronze. But the smiths found, by accident and over generations, that iron left in a charcoal fire soaks up something from the charcoal, and if you then plunge it red-hot into water, it comes out harder than anything bronze can do. That's steel. By about 900 BCE they could do it on purpose.

Think what that means for the Farmer. Bronze had always been the king's metal, because only a king could get tin. An iron plow tip, an iron axe, an iron sickle can be made in any village with a smith. The best tools in the world don't have to come from the palace any more.

I said I'd tell you why the Iron Age began. It began as a substitute. People used the metal they could get. Then it turned out that the metal anyone could get was the better one after all.

And the Counter. This is the fourth question and the best thing in this part. Where does the alphabet come from?

Remember the miners in the Sinai desert, around 1850 BCE, scratching an ox's head on a rock to stand for the first sound of their word for ox. I told you to hold onto it.

For six hundred years after that, almost nothing happens. The idea survives among the ordinary people of Canaan, used for scribbles: a name on a pot, a few words on a dagger. Every serious scribe ignores it. Real writing is Babylonian wedges or Egyptian pictures, and it takes twelve years to learn, and that's the point of it. It keeps the profession small.

There's one of those scribbles I love. In 2016 archaeologists in Israel found a small ivory comb, the fine-toothed kind you use for lice. In 2022 someone noticed faint letters scratched on its side. If they've been read correctly, and not everyone agrees, it's the oldest full sentence ever found in an alphabet. It says: may this tusk root out the lice of the hair and the beard.

The first sentence we have in the writing system you're using right now is a wish about head lice.

Then the palaces fell, and the schools that taught the big scripts fell with them. The little script didn't need a school. A father could teach it to a son in a few weeks. So in Canaan and on the coast it's the one that's left. By about 1050 BCE the Phoenician traders have settled on a standard set of twenty-two letters, and they take it with them wherever they sail, because a merchant needs to label a jar and write a receipt.

Around 800 BCE the Greeks, who've written nothing for four hundred years, pick it up from Phoenician traders. They keep the letters in the same order and they keep the names, although the names mean nothing in Greek. Alef, the ox, becomes alpha. Bet, the house, becomes beta. They add signs for vowels, which the Phoenicians did without.

So the word alphabet is two Canaanite words: ox, house.

From the Greeks it goes to the Romans, and from the Romans to us. From the Phoenicians it also goes east, to Hebrew and Aramaic and in time to Arabic. Nearly every alphabet on Earth comes down from those miners.

It's the most important invention in this whole series, and look at who made it. It wasn't the scribes with their twelve years of training, or the kings. It was a crew of foreign laborers who couldn't read. And what gave it its chance was the collapse. As long as the palaces stood, the hard scripts had all the jobs. When the palaces went, the easy script was the one still standing.

Here's a what-if that I can't prove and can't stop turning over. Suppose the palaces had survived. The clerks keep their hold on writing. The miners' alphabet stays a scribble at the edge of the desert. Bronze stays the king's metal, and iron stays a curiosity in a royal treasury. No farmer's son in the hills ever learns his letters. I'm not saying the collapse was a good thing. A great many people died in it. But some of what you and I take for granted grew in the ground it cleared, and I don't see how it grows otherwise.

One correction before we finish, so I don't leave you with the wrong map.

Not everybody forgot. In the east, Assyria, the merchant city, came through. It shrank. It lost its outer provinces and had some very bad decades. But it kept its capital, its kings, its gods and its schools. So did Babylon. In Iraq nobody ever stopped reading. Boys were still copying out the old Sumerian word lists, the same lists that bored boy copied.

That difference decides what comes next. The west lost its memory and had to make up stories about giants. The east kept its libraries. Hold onto that, because the last part begins in one of them.

So where's the family, around 750 BCE?

Go back to the hill village and look inside one of those stone houses, early in the morning.

There's a man who works the field, and the field is his.

His sister is at the grinding stone, as she was in the first house. What she grinds stays in this house. Nobody has her on a list.

His grain is in a pit in the floor, and he's the one who decides when to open it.

When he needs an axe head he walks to the smith in the next village, who makes it from red rock out of the hillside, and he pays in olive oil.

Once or twice a year a trader comes up from the coast with a donkey, selling salt and cloth and news.

And on the shoulder of the big storage jar by the door, somebody has scratched a few letters. It's a name, his or his father's. Nobody in the house went to school. They just know the letters.

It's the first house again. The Farmer, the Keeper, the Counter, the Maker and the Carrier are back within shouting distance of each other, and most of them are the same person.

It's smaller than the world of the ship, and poorer. He'll never see blue stone from Afghanistan or hear four languages on a quay. He also doesn't need anything from the far end of the earth to get through the year.

And he has two things the first house didn't. He has a metal that doesn't need a king, and a way of writing that doesn't need a school. Out of those two things, in about three hundred years, his descendants and the Greeks' are going to build something new.

But they won't remember what came before. They'll look at the ruins and say giants. They'll tell stories about a war at a place called Troy, and about a flood, and about a baby in a basket.

So what did survive? And how, three thousand years later, did we find out what really happened? That's the last part.


# Part 9 — What Survived

You know this story too.

A beautiful queen runs off with a foreign prince. Her husband's brother, the greatest king in Greece, raises an army from every Greek kingdom and sails across the sea to get her back. They fight outside the walls of a city called Troy for ten years. The best warrior on the Greek side is a man named Achilles, who can only be hurt in one place. In the end the city is taken with a trick: a wooden horse.

That's the Trojan War. The oldest telling of it is a poem called the Iliad, and the Greeks said it was composed by a blind singer named Homer.

Here's where we are. It's about 750 BCE. The fires that ended the palaces are four hundred and fifty years in the past, about as far back from Homer as the first English settlers in America are from us. Greece has been without writing that whole time. And in those four and a half centuries the Greeks have been telling each other about a great age long ago, when kings lived in halls at Mycenae and at Pylos and wore armor made of bronze.

You've been to Pylos. It's where the clerk sat at his desk by the door, counting figs and wool. In Homer, Pylos is the home of a wise old king named Nestor, who gives long speeches and drinks from a golden cup so heavy that an ordinary man can hardly lift it.

There's no clerk in Homer, or tablets, or ration lists, or weaving women labelled "captives." Homer didn't know any of that had existed. He didn't know what he was remembering.

And yet he was remembering something, and here's how we can tell.

In the Iliad there's a passage where a warrior is lent a helmet, and the poet stops to describe it. It's a leather cap, he says, covered on the outside with rows of white tusks from wild boars, set closely together, pointing this way and that.

Nobody in Homer's day wore a helmet like that. Nobody had for about five hundred years. But archaeologists have dug them out of graves from the age of the palaces, and they look just the way the poem says.

So a description of an object passed from singer to singer for twenty generations, with no writing, long after anyone had seen the thing itself. The poem kept the helmet and the bronze swords, and it kept the names of the right hills. Everything else it replaced with what a good story needs.

First question, then. Was the Trojan War real?

There's a place. In the northwest corner of Turkey, by the straits that lead to the Black Sea, there's a mound that people have been digging since the 1870s. It was a fortified town for two thousand years, and it was destroyed and rebuilt many times. One of those destructions, by fire, comes at about the right date, a little after 1200 BCE.

That alone wouldn't prove much. But remember the Hittites, the great kingdom in central Turkey whose government walked out of its own capital and vanished. When their archives were finally read, there were letters in them about the far west of their territory. Those letters mention a town up in that corner of Turkey that the Hittites called Wilusa. An early Greek name for Troy was Wilios. They mention a king of that town named Alaksandu. In Homer, the prince who steals the queen has two names, and the other one is Alexandros. And they mention, more than once, trouble in that region with a king from across the sea, from a land the Hittites called Ahhiyawa. Homer's most common name for the Greeks is the Achaeans.

In one of those letters a Hittite king, writing to the king of that land across the sea, says that the two of them once quarreled over Wilusa, and that it's settled now.

So here's what I think. There was no ten-year siege and there was no wooden horse. But Greeks from the palaces really were fighting and meddling around a town very like Troy, in the last century before everything fell apart. And that turned, over five hundred years of retelling, into the Iliad.

I love the shape of this. The Greeks forgot the Hittites completely. They don't appear in Homer at all. And the Hittites' own filing cabinet turns out to hold the paperwork on Homer's war.

One more thing from Homer's century, and it's my favorite object in this whole series.

By about 750 the Greeks are sailing again. They've picked up the alphabet from Phoenician traders, the twenty-two letters that go back to those miners in the desert, and they've added vowels. And they've planted a trading post on an island in the Bay of Naples, eight hundred miles from home.

In a grave on that island, a boy's grave, archaeologists found a plain clay drinking cup. Somebody had scratched three lines of verse on it. It's one of the oldest pieces of Greek alphabetic writing in existence. Here's what it says.

"I am Nestor's cup, good to drink from. Whoever drinks from this cup, desire for fair-crowned Aphrodite will seize him at once."

It's a joke. Nestor's cup, in the poem, is that huge golden thing a man can hardly lift. This is a cheap clay cup at a drinking party, announcing that it's the famous one, and that it'll make you fall in love.

Think about where that cup stands in our story. Nestor is the king of Pylos. The real Pylos had a clerk, and a shelf of tablets that only a few dozen people could read, and every one of them was a list. Writing in this part of the world started as a receipt for barley, and for three thousand years it belonged to the people who kept the accounts.

Then it was lost in Greece. And when the Greeks got writing back, in an alphabet anybody could learn in a few weeks, one of the first things somebody did with it was scratch a joke about a hero on a cup, for his friends.

The counting had turned into writing a long time before. With that cup it stops belonging to the palace.

Now go east, because I told you not everybody forgot.

Remember Assur, the merchant city on the Tigris, where Lamassi wove her cloth. It came through the collapse. Over the next few centuries it grew into Assyria, the empire I described at the very beginning: the one that ruled from Iran to Egypt, with its capital at Nineveh.

Around 650 BCE the king of Assyria was a man named Ashurbanipal. He was a conqueror, and a brutal one. He was also a collector. He sent agents to every old city in Iraq with orders to find ancient tablets and copy them or bring them back. Medical texts, star charts, dictionaries, omens, prayers. He boasted that he could read the old dead language of the first cities, and inscriptions, as he put it, "from before the flood."

Among the things his scribes copied was the story of Gilgamesh, the king of Uruk, the one name that got out. By then that story was older to them than King Arthur is to us. And in it there's a chapter about a great flood, and a man who is warned by a god to build a boat and load it with animals.

That library is the end of an unbroken line. The boy with the doodles on his homework, fourteen hundred years after the first tablets, was a link in it. Every generation taught the next one the signs. In Iraq that chain never broke.

In 612 BCE Nineveh's enemies took the city and burned it. The palace came down on the library. And you know by now what fire does to clay.

Two hundred and eleven years later, a Greek soldier named Xenophon walked past a ruined wall and asked the locals who had built it.

He was standing on top of it. Under the rubble was the greatest library in the world, baked hard and perfectly legible, with the flood story in it, and the king's own boasts, and the answer to every question he asked that day.

It waited another twenty-two hundred years.

Before I tell you how we got it back, there's one inheritance that never had to be dug up, because people never stopped reading it.

I want to go carefully here. The Hebrew Bible is sacred to a great many people, and I'm talking about history, which is a different conversation from faith. But as history, it's the Bronze Age's largest surviving heir, and most people who read it don't know that.

You've met the pieces already in this series.

A baby set adrift on a river in a basket sealed with tar, who grows up to lead a nation. We met him as Sargon.

A flood sent to destroy mankind, one man warned to build a boat, the animals, the bird sent out to look for land. We met that in Iraq, a thousand years before the Bible's version was written.

The law that a man who falls into debt and has to sell himself serves for a fixed number of years and then goes free. In the Bible it's six years. On Hammurabi's pillar it's three.

The law about an ox that gores a man to death, and whether the owner knew the ox was dangerous. It's in the Bible, and it's on the pillar, in nearly the same terms.

The Jubilee, when debts are cancelled and land goes back to the families that lost it. That's the kings of Babylon breaking the tablets. The Hebrew word for that release is the same word the Babylonians used.

And the central idea, the covenant, the solemn agreement between God and the people. It's laid out in a particular order: who is making this agreement, what he has done for you, what he requires, who the witnesses are, and what happens if you break it. That's the layout of a Bronze Age treaty between a great king and a lesser one. We have dozens of them, from the Hittite archives.

Even the poetry has an ancestor. When the burned port of Ugarit was dug up, its tablets turned out to contain hymns in a language very close to Hebrew, with phrases that turn up again in the Psalms.

So the Bible didn't come from nowhere. It's what the old world of law and treaty and story looked like when it was carried forward by a small people in the hills, written in the miners' alphabet.

And there's one thing in it that I don't think is inherited from anybody. It's told from the other side. For three thousand years in this story the people at the grinding stone and in the weaving shed have been numbers in somebody else's list. The Bible's founding story is told by the slaves. It says, over and over: remember that you were slaves in Egypt. I can't tell you how much history is behind that story. But as a point of view, I don't know of anything like it in all the records that came before.

Now. How did we get the rest back?

Second question, and it's the one I'd want answered if I were you. How do we know any of this? How do you read a language that nobody has spoken for two thousand years?

Take Egypt first. We know the day its writing died. The last inscription in Egyptian picture-signs was carved on a temple wall in the far south on the twenty-fourth of August in the year 394. After that there was nobody left who could read them. For fourteen hundred years people looked at the temples of Egypt, covered in writing from floor to ceiling, and could not read a word.

In 1799 French soldiers in Napoleon's army were rebuilding an old fort in the Nile Delta and pulled a slab of dark stone out of a wall. It had the same decree carved on it three times, in three scripts. The bottom one was Greek, which scholars could read.

It still took twenty-three years. The man who did it was a Frenchman named Jean-François Champollion, who'd been obsessed with Egypt since he was a boy. He had one advantage. He'd learned Coptic, the language still used in the churches of Egypt, which is the last descendant of what the pharaohs spoke.

The key was names. The Greek text mentioned a king, Ptolemy. In the Egyptian text some groups of signs were enclosed in ovals. If the ovals held royal names, then those signs had to be spelling out sounds, because you can't draw a picture of "Ptolemy." He matched the signs in that oval with another name from another monument, Cleopatra. The P, the T, the O and the L turned up in both, in the right places.

From those few letters he worked outward. On a September day in 1822 he ran down the street to his brother's office, shouted "I've got it!" and collapsed. By the family's account he was in bed for five days.

The wedge writing was harder, because there was no Greek to start from.

The break came from a cliff. In western Iran, on the old road from Babylon up into the mountains, a king of Persia had his victories carved into a rock face three hundred feet above the ground, in about 520 BCE. He had it done in three languages, all in wedge-shaped signs, so that all his subjects could read it. Then he had the ledge below cut away so nobody could deface it.

In the 1830s a young British army officer named Henry Rawlinson was posted nearby, and he decided to copy it. He did it standing on the top rung of a ladder balanced on a ledge eighteen inches wide, holding on with one hand and writing with the other. For the worst section he hired a local boy who climbed across the bare rock on ropes and pegs and took paper impressions.

One of the three languages was Old Persian, a relative of languages scholars already knew, and it was cracked first, again through kings' names. That gave them the meaning of the whole text. Then, sign by sign, they worked out the version in Babylonian, the language of Hammurabi and the kings' letters.

And a lot of people didn't believe it. The script had hundreds of signs, and the same sign could be read several ways. It looked like guesswork. So in 1857 a learned society in London ran a test. A long inscription of an Assyrian king had just been dug up, and nobody had published it. Copies went to four scholars who claimed they could read the script. Each worked alone and sent his translation back in a sealed envelope.

The envelopes were opened together. The four translations agreed.

That's the day I'd point to if someone asked how we know. Everything I've read you from clay in this series rests on a method that passed that test.

By then the tablets were arriving. In the 1840s and 50s two men dug into the mounds at Nineveh. One was an Englishman, Austen Henry Layard. The other was his assistant, Hormuzd Rassam, who was born in the town right across the river and deserves to be better known. Between them they found the rooms of Ashurbanipal's library, the tablets lying in heaps where the shelves had burned out from under them. Some thirty thousand pieces went to the British Museum in London.

And there they sat, because there were perhaps a dozen people alive who could read them.

One who taught himself was a young Londoner named George Smith. He'd left school at fourteen to be apprenticed to a firm that engraved banknotes. He spent his lunch hours in the museum looking at the tablets, and he got so good at reading them that the museum hired him to sort the fragments.

In 1872 he was working through a broken tablet and found himself reading about a ship coming to rest on a mountain, and a dove being sent out to look for dry land.

A colleague who was in the room wrote down what happened. Smith read down the lines, and said: "I am the first man to read that after more than two thousand years of oblivion." Then, and I'm quoting, "he jumped up and rushed about the room in a great state of excitement, and, to the astonishment of those present, began to undress himself."

He'd found the flood. Written in Iraq, long before the Bible, in the library Xenophon walked over.

Now you're going to read a dead language yourself.

In 1906 German archaeologists began digging at the Hittite capital in central Turkey, the one the court abandoned. They found ten thousand tablets in the first seasons. The script was the familiar wedge writing, so they could pronounce every word. Some tablets were in Babylonian, and those they could read. But most were in a language nobody had ever seen.

A Czech scholar named Bedřich Hrozný copied a stack of them in Istanbul just before the First World War. Then he was drafted. He went on working at it in uniform. And in 1915 he was looking at one sentence.

It had a sign in it that every scholar of this script knew, a sign borrowed from the old language of Uruk, and it means bread. So the sentence was about bread. Here's the rest of it, as it sounds.

Bread. Ezzatteni. Watar. Ekutteni.

Ezzatteni. He thought of the German word for eat, essen. Latin, edo. English, eat.

Watar.

"You will eat bread. And you will drink water."

The Hittites, the forgotten empire, spoke a language from the same family as English. Water is water. It's the oldest written relative of our own language that there is, and you just read it.

That leaves the Greeks, and the clerk at Pylos.

The palace at Pylos was found in 1939. On the first day of digging, the first trench went straight into the archive room, and out came the tablets that the fire had baked. Nobody could read them. Nobody knew what language they were in. Most experts were sure it wasn't Greek.

Two people broke it, and one of them rarely gets the credit.

Alice Kober taught Latin and Greek at a college in Brooklyn, and in the evenings she worked on the script. She refused to guess at the language. She just analyzed the patterns. It was wartime and paper was short, so she cut her index cards from old greeting cards and church circulars, a hundred and eighty thousand of them, and filed them in empty cigarette cartons. From those cards she proved that the words in the tablets changed their endings in regular ways, the way Latin does, and she worked out which signs had to share a consonant. She died in 1950, at forty-three, with the work unfinished.

The man who finished it was an English architect named Michael Ventris. He'd been fascinated by the script since he was fourteen. He took Kober's method and built it out into a grid, with every sign placed by which consonant and which vowel it must contain, before he knew what any of the sounds were. Then he tried fitting place names from Crete into the grid. And the words that came out, to his own astonishment, were Greek.

He announced it on the radio in July 1952. The tablets, he said, were written in "a difficult and archaic Greek, seeing that it's five hundred years older than Homer, and written in a rather abbreviated form, but Greek nevertheless."

Plenty of scholars didn't believe that either. Then a new tablet came out of the ground at Pylos, one Ventris had never seen. It was a list of pots. Beside each entry the clerk had drawn a little picture. Next to a drawing of a cauldron with three legs were signs that, by Ventris's grid, read ti-ri-po. Tripod. Next to a cup with four handles: four-eared. Next to a cup with none: no-eared.

So the people of the palaces were Greeks. Homer's heroes were real people's great-great-grandfathers. And what those people wrote down, in their own hand, was pots and sheep.

Ventris was killed in a car crash four years later. He was thirty-four.

There's a hero in all of those stories that isn't a person. It's mud.

Clay is the cheapest thing anyone ever wrote on. It's riverbank dirt. And it has outlasted everything invented since. Nanni's complaint about bad copper has survived longer than every empire that ever taxed him. Papyrus rots, parchment burns, and ink fades. When you burn a clay tablet you make it permanent.

Compare this. In 1986, to mark nine hundred years since the Domesday Book, the great survey of England made in 1086, the BBC produced a new one. A million people contributed. It was published on the most advanced medium of the day, the laser disc.

Within fifteen years it was almost unreadable. The discs were fine. The machines that played them had stopped being made, and so had the computers that ran them. It took a rescue team, working with a few surviving players, to get the data out.

The original Domesday Book is nine hundred years old. It's ink on sheepskin. You can go and read it.

Nearly everything our world writes is stored in forms that have to be copied to something new every few years, by a chain of people and machines that mustn't break. That works very well for as long as nothing interrupts it.

The Bronze Age is what an interruption looks like.

So let me try to answer the question I gave you at the start. How do people build a world that connected, live in it for centuries, and then lose it so completely that their descendants stand on the ruins and guess?

Here's what I think the story shows. I've got four things.

The first: every connection that made them richer was also something they depended on. The smith with the best metal in history couldn't work without a ship from one direction and a caravan from another. Nobody chose that. It built up one sensible decision at a time, like farming.

The second: a strong system hides its own trouble. The stores, the treaties and the alliances all existed to absorb shocks. So each shock was absorbed, and from inside it looked like nothing was wrong, right up until the reserves ran out.

The third: when it broke, what saved people wasn't courage or wisdom. It was how much they could still do for themselves. Egypt had its river. The hill farmers had their terraces. The little ports had their ships. The clerk at Pylos had a skill with one customer.

And the fourth: memory lasts only where something keeps carrying it. In Iraq it was a school that never closed. In Greece it was a song. In the Bible it was a people who kept reading. Everywhere else it took fire, clay, and somebody stubborn enough to give a life to a puzzle.

Is our world like theirs? In one way, more than I'm comfortable with. You and I depend on strangers on the far side of the planet for things we couldn't make if our lives depended on it, and it doesn't feel like a system to us either.

In another way it's completely different, and this is what I most want to leave you with. Xenophon stood on Nineveh and got a story about thunder. The herder under the walls of Tiryns said giants. Every people in this story looked back at the ruins and guessed, and guessed wrong.

We read the mail. We know the names of the three dry years. We know what the clerk at Pylos wrote in his last season and what a king of the Hittites said to his gods about a plague. Nobody before us could do that. I think it's the one new thing we have, and I'd like to believe it counts for something.

I'll finish with the one we can't read.

Far to the east of everything in this story, on the Indus River, there were cities with straight streets and covered drains, laid out before Hammurabi was born. Their people traded with Iraq. A man in Sargon's day made his living as their interpreter. And they wrote, on little squares of carved stone, in a script of a few hundred signs.

Nobody can read it. There's no Rosetta Stone for it, no cliff with three languages. Those cities faded around 1900 BCE, and whatever they wrote about themselves is still shut.

So there's a civilization as large as Egypt that we know only from the outside, the way Xenophon knew Nineveh. We know they built those walls, and we don't know one thing they said.

Somewhere there's a mound nobody has dug, with a library in it nobody can read yet. We walk past it the way he walked past his.
